Food Producers on the Front Lines

As an environmental justice advocate, I am deeply troubled by where and how we’re building the backbone of our digital future. The physical infrastructure of AI is increasingly dropped into places that can’t absorb the costs.

Rural Mason County, Kentucky, is a case in point. Farmers and residents here are fighting a proposed hyperscale data center project that could consume thousands of acres of farmland deeply tied to the region’s agricultural identity and generational heritage.

Unlike traditional data centers, which are generally 100,000 square feet or less, hyperscale data centers are massive facilities that can cover 200,000 to several million square feet and consume as much energy as some cities or even U.S. states. They house thousands of servers and support cloud computing, artificial intelligence, and other large-scale digital services.
Farmers here have reportedly been offered millions of dollars for their land, but many have refused.
You can’t get food out of a data center
,” local farmer Ida Huddleston told People. “
Everything comes from the land. Once you tear it up, you can never replace it again
.” She and her family ultimately declined a $26 million offer for their land.
“Everything comes from the land. Once you tear it up, you can never replace it again.”

Community members, including farmer and Germantown City Commissioner Max Moran, have warned in a recent podcast that the proposed hyperscale data center could impact roughly 2,100 acres of productive farmland, and if the zoning changes are approved, other centers are poised to follow, potentially impacting as many as 10,000 acres here.

They say data centers threaten not only water resources, energy infrastructure, and quality of life there, but also the long-term survival of family farming. They worry about the project’s limited transparency, too—some city officials signed nondisclosure agreements—and the noise and traffic.

For Moran, the fight is deeply personal. When interviewed for the podcast, he stood on land his family has farmed for at least six generations, reflecting on a heritage that stretches back further than he can trace.
Money isn’t everything, and the real value when it comes to the land is being able to pass it down to your next generation
“I think people should know that it’s taking up a lot of the farmland where their food comes from,” Jonathan Bowles, a Mason County fifth-grader, told WCPO 9 news.

Data center impacts are inherently local. Therefore, community engagement beyond public comment periods is key. Counties and municipalities, for example, should work with community-led organizations to establish data-center oversight boards. These boards should bring together  residents and representatives from permitting, environmental, and public health agencies, local universities, and community-based organizations.

The tension unfolding in Mason County and across the country illustrates a fundamental truth:
Technological progress should not come at the expense of community survival.

We do not have to choose between innovation and nourishment, technology and equity, or progress and public health. We only have to choose to plan wisely and listen to the communities who have always understood that the land beneath their feet, the water they drink, and the food they grow are worth more than anything a data center can offer.

Because land investors frequently export crops without providing adequate employment, this represents an effective income loss for local communities.
